name: Shrove Sunday
description: The last Sunday before Lent. Transition from celebration to repentance.
biblicalBasis: Jesus' third prediction of his suffering: 'The Son of Man will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, insulted, spat upon, flogged and killed, and on the third day he will rise again' (Luke 18:31-34; Mark 10:32-34). The blind Bartimaeus who cries out and does not give up: 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' (Mark 10:46-52). Paul's words about the way of love (1 Corinthians 13).
significance: The transition from the joy of Epiphany to the seriousness of Lent. Jesus' prediction of his suffering sets the course toward Jerusalem and the cross. Bartimaeus' cry is a picture of humanity's fundamental need for grace—he sees his own blindness and cries out for help. Discipleship costs, but begins with recognizing one's need.
liturgicalContext: Violet color. The name 'Shrove Sunday' (fastelaven = fast evening) indicates that the day is the threshold to Lent. In folk tradition it was a feast day with carnival and 'striking the cat from the barrel'—the last celebration before the seriousness of Lent.
history: The Shrovetide celebration has roots in the medieval carnival (carne vale = 'farewell to meat') before Ash Wednesday. The Lutheran church kept the Sunday but removed the carnival elements, emphasizing the prediction of suffering and the theme of discipleship.
otConnections: Isaiah 53 about the Lord's suffering servant as a background motif for the prediction of suffering. Blindness as a metaphor—Isaiah 42:18-19: 'Hear, you deaf! Look, you blind!' The transition recalls Israel's move from the celebration in the wilderness to the seriousness of the journey.

references.reason: The day marks the transition to Lent and Jesus' first public act: his baptism. The text describes Jesus' baptism, the descent of the Spirit, and the voice from heaven, which is the beginning of Jesus' public ministry and preparation for his forty days in the wilderness (read on the First Sunday of Lent).

Verses 12-25 describe the transition from John's imprisonment to Jesus' public preaching, the calling of disciples, and the first miracles. This marks the beginning of Jesus' work and the introduction to his message of repentance, which is a central theme in the transition from celebration to Lent. The extension to verse 25 captures the entire introduction to Jesus' ministry in Galilee.

The call to be 'salt and light' (vv. 13-16) and the ethical appeal for a radically new life (vv. 17-48) are central to the transition from celebration to repentance. The text calls for a visible Christian life and preparation for Lent through a deeper righteousness.

As a transitional day from celebration to repentance, Matthew 6:16-18 points to the right attitude toward fasting. It reminds us that Lent is not about outward signs of piety (a gloomy face) but about inner preparation for Easter.

The day marks the transition from celebration to repentance and preparation for Lent. The text about the narrow gate and the difficult path leading to life reminds us that discipleship requires choice and willingness to take a different path than the world's broad way, which is central to Lent's call to repentance.

The text contains Jesus' statement: 'It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick' (vv. 12-13). This is a key text for Shrove Sunday, marking the transition from celebration to repentance and emphasizing humanity's fundamental need for God's grace and healing.

Matthew 16:24-26 with the call to 'take up your cross' and 'deny yourself' is a central text for Lent and repentance. It defines discipleship as a path through suffering and self-denial. Although this is often read on Shrove Sunday, its primary liturgical context here is the introduction to the Transfiguration of Christ; therefore, in this specific tagging, the relevance is secondary.

The day marks the transition from celebration to repentance. Matthew 18:1-14 contains Jesus' call to repentance ('turn and become like children'), humility, and a stern warning against letting sin lead to falling (hand, foot, eye). This is a classic Lenten text that calls for self-examination and cleaning up one's own life before Lent, which is the core of Shrovetide themes.

The story of the rich young man is a strong appeal to repentance and giving up earthly goods to follow Jesus. This is a central theme for Shrove Sunday, marking the transition from celebration to repentance and self-examination. The text challenges the reader to consider what is most important in life.
